texts.description: Obadiah chapter 1. Both the manuscript page scan AND the Greek text are taken directly from Codex Sinaiticus (4th century AD) via the Codex Sinaiticus Project (codexsinaiticus.org). English translation verbatim from the King James Version (1611, public domain) via bible-api.com.

texts.title: Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 436-525: the arts Prometheus gave to mankind
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 32.9 (Medicean Aeschylus) fol. 152v-153v via Teca digitale BML + Smyth Greek (Perseus) + Smyth English (Loeb 1922, archive.org scan)
texts.description: Prometheus, chained to his rock, tells the chorus how mankind lived like shapes in dreams until he gave them the stars, numbers, letters, the yoke, ships, medicine, divination and metals: 'every art possessed by man comes from Prometheus'. Shown on the 10th-century Medicean manuscript, Laur. Plut. 32.9.

texts.title: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 10.6-10.8: happiness and the life of the mind as a divine life
texts.source: Laur. Plut. 81.11 fol. 121v-124v (Teca Digitale, 10th c.) and Paris gr. 1854 fol. 175r-177v (Gallica, 12th c.) + Bywater Greek (Perseus) + H. Rackham English (Perseus)
texts.description: Aristotle's argument that the highest happiness is the activity of contemplation, a life 'higher than the human level' lived by the divine element in us: 'we ought so far as possible to achieve immortality' (1177b33). Shown on the oldest manuscript, Laur. Plut. 81.11 (10th c.), with its missing text supplied from Paris gr. 1854.

texts.title: Aristotle, Metaphysics 12.6-10 (Lambda): the unmoved mover and the life of god
texts.source: Paris gr. 1853 fol. 293r-296v (Gallica, 10th c.) + Ross Greek (Perseus) + W. D. Ross English (1928, MIT Internet Classics Archive)
texts.description: Aristotle's account of the first principle: an eternal, unmoved substance whose activity is thought thinking itself; 'the actuality of thought is life, and God is that actuality' (1072b). Shown on Paris gr. 1853, a 10th-century manuscript.

texts.title: Pliny the Elder, Natural History 2.205: lands taken by the sea, 'if we believe Plato' in the Atlantic

texts.title: Berossus, Babyloniaka book 1: Oannes and the creation (Alexander Polyhistor in George Syncellus)
texts.source: Paris gr. 1711 (George Syncellus, 11th c.) via Gallica + Greek of C. Müller, FHG (DFHG, proofread) + English of I. P. Cory, Ancient Fragments (1832)
texts.description: Berossus' account, as summarized by Alexander Polyhistor and copied by George Syncellus, of the records kept at Babylon, the fish-man Oannes who taught writing, cities, laws and agriculture, and the creation of the world by Bel from the body of Omoroka, shown on the two pages of Paris gr. 1711 that carry it.

texts.title: Berossus, Babyloniaka book 2: the ten kings and the flood of Xisouthros (Alexander Polyhistor in George Syncellus)
texts.source: Paris gr. 1711 (George Syncellus, 11th c.) via Gallica + Greek of C. Müller, FHG (DFHG, proofread) + English of I. P. Cory, Ancient Fragments (1832)
texts.description: Berossus on the ten kings who reigned 120 sars (432,000 years) before the flood and on Xisouthros, warned by Kronos in a dream, who buried the writings at Sippar, built a ship, sent out birds and was taken to live with the gods, shown on the two pages of Paris gr. 1711 that carry it.

texts.title: The tower of Babel in Alexander Polyhistor (the Sibyl) and Abydenus (George Syncellus)
texts.source: Paris gr. 1711 (George Syncellus, 11th c.) via Gallica + Greek of C. Müller, FHG (DFHG, proofread) + English of I. P. Cory, Ancient Fragments (1832)
texts.description: Two Greek accounts of the tower of Babylon copied by George Syncellus from the Babylonian tradition: Alexander Polyhistor quoting the Sibyl on a single language, a tower to heaven overthrown by winds, and Titan and Prometheus after the flood; and Abydenus on the first men, proud of their strength, whose tower was thrown down by the winds and who were given many languages, shown on the page of Paris gr. 1711 that carries them.

texts.title: Berossus in Apollodorus: the ten kings before the flood and the fish-men Annedotoi (George Syncellus)
texts.source: Paris gr. 1711 (George Syncellus, 11th c.) via Gallica + Greek of C. Müller, FHG (DFHG, proofread) + English of I. P. Cory, Ancient Fragments (1832)
texts.description: Apollodorus' list, from Berossus, of the ten Chaldean kings from Aloros to Xisouthros with their reigns in sars, and of the fish-men (Oannes, the Annedotoi, Odakon) who came up from the Red Sea, shown on the two pages of Paris gr. 1711 that carry it.

texts.title: Berossus in Abydenus: the kings of the Chaldeans and the flood of Sisithros (George Syncellus)
texts.source: Paris gr. 1711 (George Syncellus, 11th c.) via Gallica + Greek of C. Müller, FHG (DFHG, proofread) + English of I. P. Cory, Ancient Fragments (1832)
texts.description: Abydenus' retelling of Berossus in Ionic Greek: Aloros the shepherd of the people, the sar of 3,600 years, the Annedotoi who came up from the sea, and Sisithros, who hid the writings at Sippar and sailed to Armenia, shown on the page of Paris gr. 1711 that carries it.

texts.title: Berossus in Josephus, Against Apion 1.128-153: Nabopolassar, Nebuchadnezzar and the last kings of Babylon
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 69.22 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale IIIF + Niese Greek (Perseus) + Whiston English (Project Gutenberg)
texts.description: Josephus quotes Berossus' third book on Nebuchadnezzar's campaign, his building of Babylon and the hanging garden, and the kings after him down to Nabonidus and the capture of Babylon by Cyrus, shown on the four pages of the 10th-century Florence manuscript Laur. Plut. 69.22 that carry it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Prologue (obverse, columns i-v)

texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: The prologue of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE), in which Hammurabi names the gods who called him to rule and the cities he cared for, shown column by column on the Louvre stele.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 1-65 (obverse, columns v-xvi)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: Laws 1-65 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): false accusation and witnesses, judges, theft and receiving, kidnapping, runaway slaves, burglary and robbery, the fiefs of soldiers and tax-gatherers, fields, gardens, irrigation, and the leasing of orchards. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 100-149 (reverse, columns i-ix)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: Laws 100-149 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): merchants and their agents, wine-sellers, debt, pledges and deposits, slander, adultery, marriage, the wives of captives, divorce and the sick wife. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 150-199 (reverse, columns ix-xvii)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: Laws 150-199 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): gifts to wives, debts of husband and wife, incest, betrothal and the marriage settlement, dowries, inheritance, children of slave women, priestesses' shares, adoption, and bodily injury. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 200-249 (reverse, columns xvii-xxi)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)

texts.description: Laws 200-249 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): bodily injury and its payments, physicians, veterinary surgeons, branders, builders, boatmen, and hired oxen. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Laws 250-282 (reverse, columns xxi-xxiii)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: Laws 250-282 of the Code of Hammurabi (c. 1754 BCE): the goring ox, the hire of oxen, farm hands and herdsmen, theft of farm implements, wages of labourers and craftsmen, hire of boats, and the sale of slaves. Each law is shown with its Akkadian lines, Harper's English and the stele column that carries it.

texts.title: Code of Hammurabi: Epilogue (reverse, columns xxiv-xxviii)
texts.date_approx: c. 1754 BCE (stele set up late in Hammurabi's reign)
texts.source: Louvre Sb 8 photographs (Wikimedia Commons; CDLI montage) + CDLI P249253 transliteration + R. F. Harper's 1904 English
texts.description: The epilogue of the Code of Hammurabi: the king's charge to later rulers and the curses on anyone who alters the stele, shown column by column on the Louvre stele.

texts.title: Corpus Hermeticum I: Poimandres
texts.source: Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 71.33 fol. 123r-125v (Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Teca digitale (IIIF)) + Parthey's Greek (1854, Wikisource) + G. R. S. Mead's English (1906)
texts.description: The first Hermetic treatise: the vision of Poimandres, the divine Mind, on the making of the world, the fall of the archetypal Man and the soul's ascent through the seven spheres to God, shown complete on the 14th-century Florence manuscript Laur. Plut. 71.33.

texts.title: Corpus Hermeticum XIII: the Secret Discourse on the Mountain, on Rebirth
texts.source: Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 71.33 fol. 141v-144r (Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Teca digitale (IIIF)) + Parthey's Greek (1854, transcribed from the page images) + G. R. S. Mead's English (1906)
texts.description: Hermes teaches his son Tat the way of rebirth: the twelve torments of matter are driven out by ten powers of God, Tat is born again in Mind and sings the secret hymn of rebirth. Complete, shown on the 14th-century Florence manuscript Laur. Plut. 71.33.

texts.title: Counsels of Wisdom (Babylonian moral advice)
texts.date_approx: composed late 2nd millennium BCE; tablets 7th-1st c. BCE
texts.source: British Museum and Penn Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L II.3, Counsels of Wisdom (ed. Z. J. Földi), SB -) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
texts.description: The Counsels of Wisdom, text: 159 of 159 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (14 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

texts.title: Cuthaean Legend of Naram-Sin (Standard Babylonian version)
texts.date_approx: composed early 2nd millennium BCE; tablets 7th c. BCE
texts.source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.12, Cuthaean Legend of Naram-Sin (ed. T. D. N. Mitto), SB -) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
texts.description: The Cuthaean Legend of Naram-Sin, Standard Babylonian version: 175 of 180 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (5 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.

texts.title: Cyrus Cylinder, lines 6-36 (BM 90920)
texts.source: British Museum BM 90920, photographs by Prioryman on Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0) + ORACC ARIo text and translation (CC BY-SA 3.0)
texts.description: The Cyrus Cylinder (after 539 BCE), Cyrus the Great's account of his entry into Babylon and the return of the gods and peoples, lines 6-36 with ARIo's text and translation and photographs of the cylinder.

pages.caption: Cyrus Cylinder, side with lines 5-22 (turned upright)

texts.title: Diodorus Siculus 1.10-13: the first men, the eternal gods and the god-kings of Egypt
texts.source: Vat. gr. 130 (10th c.) via DigiVatLib IIIF + Vogel Greek (Perseus, checked against the 1888 printing) + Oldfather English (Loeb 1933, public domain)
texts.description: The Egyptian account in Diodorus of how the first men came into being in Egypt from the mud of the Nile, of the sun and moon as the eternal gods Osiris and Isis, of the elements as gods, and of the earthly gods who ruled Egypt as kings, from Helius or Hephaestus to Cronus and Osiris.

texts.title: Diodorus Siculus 1.44: gods and heroes for almost 18,000 years, then mortal kings
texts.source: Vat. gr. 130 (10th c.) via DigiVatLib IIIF + Vogel Greek (Perseus, checked against the 1888 printing) + Oldfather English (Loeb 1933, public domain)
texts.description: Diodorus' summary of the Egyptian priests' chronology: gods and heroes ruled Egypt for a little less than 18,000 years, the last of them Horus son of Isis, and mortal kings for almost 5,000 years, 470 men and 5 women of native birth besides the Ethiopian, Persian and Macedonian rulers.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.99-101: Min, Nitocris and the 330 kings
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: Herodotus begins the Egyptian priests' history of their kings: Min, the first king, who dammed the Nile and founded Memphis; the 330 kings after him read out from a papyrus roll, among them the queen Nitocris; and Moeris, who built the lake.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.102-110: Sesostris, the conqueror king
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: The campaigns of Sesostris by sea and land through Asia and into Europe, the pillars he set up, the Colchians as Egyptian settlers, the plot of his brother at Daphnae, the canals dug by his captives, and his statues at the temple of Hephaestus.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.111: Pheros, the blind king
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: Pheros, son of Sesostris, who threw a spear into the flooding Nile, was struck blind for ten years, and recovered his sight as the oracle of Buto foretold.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.112-120: Proteus, and Helen in Egypt
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: The priests' account of Proteus of Memphis, who detained Helen and the stolen treasure when Paris was driven to Egypt, of Menelaus' visit, and Herodotus' argument that Homer knew this version and that Helen was never at Troy.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.121-123: Rhampsinitus, the treasure-thief, and the descent to the underworld
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: Rhampsinitus and the tale of the builder's sons who robbed his treasury, his journey alive to the underworld where he played dice with Demeter, and the Egyptian teaching on the immortality and migration of the soul.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.124-128: Cheops and Chephren, the builders of the pyramids
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: Cheops, who closed the temples and set all Egyptians to building the Great Pyramid, its construction by stages and its cost in radishes, onions and garlic, and his brother Chephren's pyramid; 106 years of oppression.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.129-135: Mycerinus, the oracle of six years, and Rhodopis
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: Mycerinus, who reopened the temples and judged justly, his daughter buried in a golden cow at Sais, the oracle that gave him six more years, his pyramid, and the story of the courtesan Rhodopis.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.136: Asychis and the brick pyramid
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: Asychis, who built the eastern gateway of the temple of Hephaestus, made a law of loans on the security of a father's mummy, and built a pyramid of brick.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.137-140: Anysis the blind and Sabacos the Ethiopian
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: The blind king Anysis, the fifty-year rule of the Ethiopian Sabacos who raised the cities on mounds, his dream and withdrawal, and Anysis' return from the marshes.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.141: Sethos and the army of Sennacherib
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: Sethos, priest of Hephaestus, whose army of shopkeepers and craftsmen faced Sennacherib at Pelusium, where mice gnawed the enemy's quivers, bowstrings and shield-straps in the night.

texts.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.142-146: The priests' chronology: 341 generations and 11,340 years
texts.source: Florence, Laur. Plut. 70.3 (10th c.) via BML Teca Digitale + Greek of Godley's Loeb (Perseus) + English of A. D. Godley (1920, Wikisource, checked against the printing)
texts.description: The priests' reckoning from the first king to Sethos: 341 generations of kings and high priests, 11,340 years without a god in human form, in which the sun four times rose out of its usual place; the 345 wooden statues shown to Hecataeus at Thebes; and the ages of Heracles, Dionysus and Pan.

texts.description: Pausanias on the first-fruits of the Hyperboreans, passed by the Arimaspi, Issedones and Scythians to Sinope and through Greece to Prasiae in Attica, and taken by the Athenians to Delos (1.31.2), on Paris gr. 1410.

texts.title: Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.5.7-10: the Delphic oracle founded by men from the Hyperboreans
texts.source: Paris gr. 1410 via Gallica (BnF) + Spiro's Greek (Perseus) + Jones's English (Loeb, Perseus)
texts.description: Pausanias on Boeo's hymn, which said the oracle at Delphi was founded by Hyperboreans, Olen first among them, and on the temple of wax and feathers sent by Apollo to the Hyperboreans (10.5.7-10), on Paris gr. 1410.

texts.title: Inana's Descent to the Netherworld

texts.title: The Instructions of Shuruppak (Old Babylonian version)

texts.title: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.63-64 (Testimonium Flavianum)

texts.title: The Keš Temple Hymn (Old Babylonian version)

texts.title: Manetho on the Reigns of the Gods and Demigods (George Syncellus)
texts.date_approx: c. 280 BCE (Manetho); Syncellus c. 810 AD; manuscript 11th c.
texts.source: Paris gr. 1711 (11th c.), pp. 11-12, via Gallica IIIF + Müller FHG II Greek (DFHG, checked against the print) + Waddell English (Loeb 1940, public domain)
texts.description: Manetho's list of the gods who ruled Egypt before men, from Hephaestus (Ptah) for 9000 years to Typhon, and of the demigods Horus to Zeus, as quoted by George Syncellus, on the page of Paris gr. 1711 that carries it.

texts.title: Manetho's Dynasties I-XI (Book I), in Africanus and Eusebius (George Syncellus)
texts.date_approx: c. 280 BCE (Manetho); epitomes 3rd-4th c. AD; Syncellus c. 810 AD; manuscript 11th c.
texts.source: Paris gr. 1764 (11th c.), fols. 2r-4v, via Gallica IIIF + Müller FHG II Greek (DFHG, checked against the print) + Waddell English (Loeb 1940, public domain)
texts.description: The first book of Manetho's king list, from Menes to the Eleventh Dynasty, in the two versions of Julius Africanus and Eusebius as copied by George Syncellus, shown on the manuscript pages of Paris gr. 1764.

texts.title: Manetho's Dynasties XII-XIX (Book II): Sesostris, the Shepherd Kings, the Exodus and the Fall of Troy, in Africanus and Eusebius (George Syncellus)
texts.date_approx: c. 280 BCE (Manetho); epitomes 3rd-4th c. AD; Syncellus c. 810 AD; manuscript 11th c.
texts.source: Paris gr. 1764 (11th c.), fols. 4v-5v and 9r-10v, via Gallica IIIF + Müller FHG II Greek (DFHG, checked against the print) + Waddell English (Loeb 1940, public domain)
texts.description: The start of Manetho's second book: the Twelfth Dynasty with Sesostris, conqueror of Asia, and the builder of the Labyrinth, the Thirteenth to Seventeenth Dynasties with the Shepherd Kings (Hyksos), the Eighteenth Dynasty with Amosis and the Exodus, and the Nineteenth Dynasty, ending with Thuoris, in whose reign Troy was taken, in the versions of Africanus and Eusebius, on the manuscript pages of Paris gr. 1764.

texts.title: Manetho on the Hyksos (Josephus, Against Apion 1.73-105)
texts.date_approx: c. 280 BCE (Manetho); quoted by Josephus c. 95 AD; manuscript 10th c.
texts.source: Laur. Plut. 69.22 (10th c.), fols. 6v-8v, via BML Teca Digitale IIIF + Niese Greek (Perseus) + Whiston English (Perseus)
texts.description: Manetho's account of the Hyksos, the 'shepherd kings' who seized Egypt, and of the kings after their expulsion, quoted word for word by Josephus in Against Apion 1.73-105 and shown on the five pages of the oldest manuscript.

texts.title: Manetho on Osarseph and the Lepers (Josephus, Against Apion 1.227-251)
texts.date_approx: c. 280 BCE (Manetho); quoted by Josephus c. 95 AD; manuscript 10th c.
texts.source: Laur. Plut. 69.22 (10th c.), fols. 16r-18r, via BML Teca Digitale IIIF + Niese Greek (Perseus) + Whiston English (Perseus, checked against the 1860 printing)
texts.description: Manetho's story of King Amenophis, the lepers sent to the quarries, the priest Osarseph who led them in revolt from Avaris and was later called Moses, and the thirteen years of their rule, as quoted by Josephus in Against Apion 1.227-251.

texts.title: Manetho's Dynasties XX-XXXI (Book III), in Africanus and Eusebius (George Syncellus)
texts.date_approx: c. 280 BCE (Manetho); epitomes 3rd-4th c. AD; Syncellus c. 810 AD; manuscript 11th c.
texts.source: Paris gr. 1764 (11th c.), fols. 10v-11v, via Gallica IIIF + Müller FHG II Greek (DFHG, checked against the print) + Waddell English (Loeb 1940, public domain)
texts.description: The third book of Manetho's king list, from the Twentieth Dynasty to the Persian kings conquered by Alexander, in the versions of Africanus and Eusebius as copied by George Syncellus, on the manuscript pages of Paris gr. 1764.

texts.title: Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone), Louvre AO 5066

Shown on the 11th-century manuscript Laur. Plut. 36.12.

texts.title: The Instruction of Ptahhotep (Papyrus Prisse, complete)

texts.date_approx: Middle Kingdom composition; manuscript c. 1650-1550 BCE

texts.title: Philo of Alexandria, On the Creation of the World (De opificio mundi)
texts.source: Vatican City, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Pal. gr. 248 fol. 40v-56v (Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, DigiVatLib (IIIF)) + Cohn-Wendland Greek (First1KGreek) + C. D. Yonge English (1854, First1KGreek)
texts.description: Philo's account of the six days of creation read as philosophy: God first conceives the intelligible world in his Logos, then makes the visible world after it; man is made in the image of God as to his mind. Complete, shown on the pages of the Vatican manuscript Pal. gr. 248.

texts.title: Philo of Alexandria, On the Confusion of Tongues 146-147: the Logos, God's firstborn and image
texts.source: Vatican City, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Pal. gr. 248 fol. 205r (Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, DigiVatLib (IIIF)) + Cohn-Wendland Greek (First1KGreek) + C. D. Yonge English (1854, First1KGreek)
texts.description: Philo on the Logos as God's first-born, the eldest of the angels, an archangel of many names, called the Beginning, the Name of God, the Man after God's image and he who sees, Israel; whoever is not yet fit to be called a son of God may be a son of his image, the Logos. Shown on Pal. gr. 248 fol. 205r.

texts.title: Philo of Alexandria, Who is the Heir of Divine Things 205-206: the Logos stands between Creator and creation
texts.source: Vatican City, Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Pal. gr. 248 fol. 293r (Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, DigiVatLib (IIIF)) + Cohn-Wendland Greek (First1KGreek) + C. D. Yonge English (1854, First1KGreek)
texts.description: Philo on the archangel and eldest Logos, who stands on the border between the Creator and what he made, a suppliant for mortals and an ambassador of the ruler, 'neither being uncreate as God, nor yet created as you'. Shown on Pal. gr. 248 fol. 293r.

texts.title: Plato, Theaetetus 172c-177c: the philosopher and the flight to become like god
texts.source: Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS. E. D. Clarke 39 fol. 96v-99r (Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford, Digital Bodleian (IIIF)) + Burnet Greek (Perseus) + H. N. Fowler (1921) English (Perseus)
texts.description: The digression of the Theaetetus, where Socrates says that we should flee from here to there, and that the flight is becoming like god as far as possible (176a-b), shown on the pages of the Clarke Plato (895 AD) that carry it.

texts.title: Plato, Symposium 201d-212c: Diotima on love and the ascent to beauty itself
texts.source: Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS. E. D. Clarke 39 fol. 213r-218r (Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford, Digital Bodleian (IIIF)) + Burnet Greek (Perseus) + W. R. M. Lamb (1925) English (Perseus)
texts.description: Socrates' report of what the priestess Diotima taught him about love: love as a spirit between gods and mortals, the desire to possess the good for ever, and the ascent from one beautiful body to beauty itself, shown on the Clarke Plato (895 AD).

texts.title: Plato, Laws 4.715e-716d: god is the measure of all things
texts.source: Paris, Bibliotheque nationale de France, grec 1807 fol. 189v (Bibliotheque nationale de France, Gallica (IIIF)) + Burnet Greek (Perseus) + R. G. Bury (1926) English (Perseus)
texts.description: The Athenian Stranger's address to the new colonists in Laws book 4: god holds the beginning, end and middle of all things; god, not man, is the measure of all things; and the one who would be dear to god must become like him. Shown on Paris gr. 1807, fol. 189v (9th c.).

texts.title: Plato, Phaedrus 245c-250c: the immortal soul, the winged chariot and the place beyond the heavens
texts.source: Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS. E. D. Clarke 39 fol. 232v-235r (Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford, Digital Bodleian (IIIF)) + Burnet Greek (Perseus) + H. N. Fowler (1914) English (Perseus)
texts.description: Socrates' proof that every soul is immortal because it moves itself, followed by the myth of the soul as a winged chariot that follows the gods to the place beyond the heavens, where it sees true being; shown on the Clarke Plato (895 AD).

texts.title: Plato, Phaedo 78b-84b: the soul's kinship with the divine
texts.source: Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS. E. D. Clarke 39 fol. 37r-40v (Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford, Digital Bodleian (IIIF)) + Burnet Greek (Perseus) + H. N. Fowler (1914) English (Perseus)
texts.description: Socrates on his last day argues that the soul is most like the divine, immortal and unchanging, and the body most like the mortal; the soul that has practised philosophy goes at death to what is like itself, the divine; shown on the Clarke Plato (895 AD).

texts.title: Plato, Laws 3.676a-679e: the floods and the survivors on the mountains
texts.source: Paris gr. 1807 (9th c.) via Gallica + Burnet Greek (Perseus) + Bury English (Loeb 1926, Perseus)
texts.description: The Athenian stranger on the vast age of human society: thousands of cities founded and destroyed, floods and plagues that left only a few herdsmen alive on the mountain tops, the loss of all arts and tools, and the simple, peaceful and honest life of the survivors, shown on the pages of Paris gr. 1807 that carry it.

texts.title: Plato, Laws 3.680a-683a: from households to cities, Troy and the Dorians
texts.source: Paris gr. 1807 (9th c.) via Gallica + Burnet Greek (Perseus) + Bury English (Loeb 1926, Perseus)
texts.description: How government grew again after the flood: rule by the eldest in scattered households like Homer's Cyclopes, larger settlements in the foothills with the first lawgivers, the city in the plain at Troy, the Trojan War and the return of the exiles as Dorians, shown on the pages of Paris gr. 1807 that carry it.

texts.title: Plato, Republic 6.506d-511e: the Sun and the Divided Line
texts.source: Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 80.19 fol. 72v-75r (Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Teca digitale (IIIF)) + Burnet's Greek (Perseus) + Paul Shorey's English (Loeb, 1935, Perseus)
texts.description: Socrates' images of the Good: the sun, offspring of the Good, gives the visible world light and growth as the Good gives the intelligible world truth and being, itself 'beyond being'; then the line divided into four parts, from images to intelligence. Shown on the 12th-century Florence manuscript Laur. Plut. 80.19.

texts.title: Plato, Republic 7.514a-521b: the Allegory of the Cave
texts.source: Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 80.19 fol. 75r-78v (Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Teca digitale (IIIF)) + Burnet's Greek (Perseus) + Paul Shorey's English (Loeb, 1935, Perseus)
texts.description: The opening of Republic book 7: prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows; one is freed, turned round and dragged up into the sunlight, sees the sun itself, and must go back down. Education as the turning of the soul, and the duty of the philosopher to return. Shown on the 12th-century Florence manuscript Laur. Plut. 80.19.

texts.title: Suetonius, Nero 16.2: 'punishment was inflicted on the Christians'

texts.title: Sanchuniathon and Philo of Byblos: Porphyry's testimony and Philo's preface (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.9.20-30)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: Eusebius introduces Sanchuniathon of Berytus, older than the Trojan War, whose Phoenician History Philo of Byblos translated into Greek; Porphyry's testimony that he drew on the records of the priest Hierombalus; and Philo's preface on Taautus, inventor of writing, and on the later priests who turned history into allegory.

texts.title: Sanchuniathon: the Phoenician cosmogony and the first worship (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.1-8)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: The beginning of all things in Philo's translation of Sanchuniathon: dark air and chaos, the wind's desire, Mot and the egg-shaped Zophasemin, the 'observers of heaven', thunder waking the first living things, and the first men who worshipped the plants of the earth and the sun as Beelsamen, lord of heaven.

texts.title: Sanchuniathon: the first generations and the inventors of the arts (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.9-14)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: The generations after Aeon and Protogonus: Light, Fire and Flame who discovered fire, the giants who gave their names to Lebanon and Mount Cassius, Hypsuranius who built huts at Tyre and Ousoos who first went to sea, Chrysor who invented iron-working and sailing, the builders of brick, the shepherds, Misor and Sydyk who found salt, and Taautus who invented writing.

texts.title: Sanchuniathon: Uranus, Ge and the reign of Kronos (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.15-30)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: Uranus and Ge, the war of their son Elus or Kronos against his father, the founding of Byblos as the first city, the baetyls or living stones, the children of Kronos and Astarte, Dagon who found grain and the plough, and the mutilation of Uranus near springs and rivers.

texts.title: Sanchuniathon: Astarte, the deeds of Kronos and the symbols of Taautus (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.31-41)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: Astarte with the head of a bull and the star she found and dedicated at Tyre, Kronos' sacrifice of his only son and his gifts of cities, the four eyes and six wings Taautus devised as the insignia of Kronos, the gift of Egypt to Taautus, the records kept by the Cabeiri, and Philo's complaint that the Greeks turned these stories into myth.

texts.title: Philo of Byblos on Taautus, royal sacrifice and the serpent, with Eusebius' conclusion (Eusebius, Praeparatio evangelica 1.10.42-55)
texts.date_approx: c. 100 AD (Philo of Byblos); c. 313 AD (Eusebius); 914 AD (Paris gr. 451)
texts.source: Paris gr. 451 (Arethas codex, 914 AD) via Gallica + Dindorf Greek (First1KGreek, proofread) + Gifford English (1903)
texts.description: Further passages of Philo: Taautus who first set religion in order, the ancient custom of sacrificing a ruler's beloved son in times of danger, and the serpent, which Taautus held divine, the good daemon of the Phoenicians and the Egyptian Kneph, followed by Eusebius' closing words on the Phoenician theology.

texts.title: Virgil, Eclogue 4: the return of the golden age
texts.source: Vat. lat. 3867 (Vergilius Romanus) fol. 9v-11r (DigiVatLib) + Greenough Latin (Perseus) + James Rhoades (1921) English (Perseus)
texts.description: Virgil's fourth Eclogue, written around 40 BCE: the last age foretold by the Sibyl has come, the Virgin returns and a new race is sent down from heaven, and a child is born under whom the iron age will end and the golden age return. Shown on the Vergilius Romanus (5th century).

texts.title: Virgil, Aeneid 6.724-751: Anchises on the world-soul and the return of souls
texts.source: Vat. lat. 3225 (Vergilius Vaticanus) fol. 55r-55v (DigiVatLib) + Greenough Latin (Perseus) + Theodore C. Williams (1910) English (Perseus)
texts.description: In the underworld Anchises explains to Aeneas that one spirit and mind move the whole universe, that souls have a fiery heavenly origin dulled by the body, and that after purification they drink of Lethe and return to bodies. Shown on the Vergilius Vaticanus (about 400).
